overview: The Kamakura period brought Japan's first warrior government. The shogunate at Kamakura ruled beside the old court in Kyoto, the samurai became the ruling class, and new Buddhist schools, Zen among them, reached both warriors and common people.

items.text: Eisai brought Rinzai Zen from Song China, and Dogen founded Soto Zen in 1227; meditation and discipline appealed to the warriors.
Honen's Pure Land school, then Shinran's True Pure Land and Nichiren's Lotus school of 1253, offered salvation to ordinary people.
Warrior ideals of loyalty and service took shape, later codified as bushido.
Unkei and the Kei school carved lifelike portraits of monks and guardian figures with inlaid crystal eyes.
The Great Buddha of Kamakura, a bronze Amida more than 11 meters high, was cast.
Emaki handscrolls told war tales and temple legends; ink painting arrived with the Zen monks.
Samurai held land as vassals of the shogun and lived by the sword and the bow.
The court in Kyoto kept its ceremonies and titles while Kamakura held the armies and the law.
Mongol invasion fleets were repelled in 1274 and 1281, the second wrecked by a typhoon later called the kamikaze.
Shoguns governed Japan for nearly 700 years, until 1868.
Zen shaped Japanese gardens, tea, ink painting and the martial arts.

fall.text: Forces loyal to Emperor Go-Daigo took Kamakura in 1333. Ashikaga Takauji turned on the emperor and set up a new shogunate in Kyoto in 1336, the start of the Muromachi period.
